episode.lensDescription: Examine complexity and tradeoffs. Surface the questions worth asking.
episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, March 30th, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, a new survey reveals the complex relationship students have with A.I. as both a learning tool and a source of anxiety. According to Inside Higher Ed, a Packback survey of nearly seven hundred college students found that roughly 5 percent said they always or often use A.I. to generate a full assignment, comparable to pre-A.I. contract cheating rates. However, nearly three-quarters of students are at least moderately concerned about being wrongly accused of using A.I., including more than 40 percent who described it as a major concern.

The survey found that about a quarter of students said they often use A.I. to support coursework such as summarizing books and articles, while roughly three times as many believe their peers are doing so. Students cited time constraints as the primary reason for using A.I. shortcuts, with 46 percent reporting this factor, while 43 percent said they didn't know enough about the topic and 42 percent lacked interest. About two-thirds of respondents said A.I. helps them grasp complex topics and deepen their understanding, while more than half said it aids them in overcoming academic obstacles. Students in business and management use A.I. more frequently across academic tasks and report more significant benefits, while students in social sciences and humanities were less likely to use A.I. often and reported fewer benefits.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. today, more than seven hundred students, faculty and staff at the University of Colorado Boulder have signed a dissent letter questioning the CU system's two million dollar agreement with OpenAI. According to GovTech, the letter raises concerns over data privacy, academic integrity, student input and A.I. governance regarding the campuswide access to ChatGPT Edu. While the university's agreement prohibits OpenAI from using data generated within the CU environment to train its public large language models, critics say the language is vague enough to raise concerns about de-identified data potentially being used for research or product improvement. Aaron Gluck, a Ph.D. student at CU Boulder researching machine learning in educational contexts who helped write the letter, said the issue is introducing A.I. in an environment where there's already misuse and limited education about proper use. The letter calls for more explicit limits on data use, transparent auditing processes, and pedagogical policies including A.I. literacy training materials.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Ethical A.I., researchers at Stanford University found that A.I. tutors produce varied feedback depending on perceived student identity and background. According to EdTech Innovation Hub, the study tested how large language models respond to variations in race, gender, achievement level, and English language proficiency across simulated student profiles. Students identified as high-achieving or White were more likely to receive detailed, development-focused feedback including critique of argumentation and suggestions for improving reasoning. In contrast, responses associated with Hispanic students or English language learners focused more heavily on grammar, spelling, and formality, reducing attention on higher-order thinking and content development. For students labeled as low-achieving or having learning disabilities, the study found a pattern of feedback withholding bias, where A.I. tutors provided positive reinforcement with limited critical input, resulting in less actionable guidance. The findings raise questions about whether consistency of learning support can be guaranteed as A.I. tutors are integrated into educational platforms.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Insights and Trends, the Texas A&M University System is launching a targeted A.I. intervention to support Pell-eligible first-year students across six diverse campuses. According to The EDU Ledger, the initiative uses chatbots to provide automated, twenty-four seven guidance, with data showing students engage most between 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. when no staff would be available. System leaders meet weekly to share insights about student engagement with the bots, which help with everything from class registration and course exchanges to emergency grant referrals and mental health triaging. The strategy aims to offload high-volume transactional hurdles like registration challenges and financial aid complexities, allowing university staff to focus on high-touch transformational interventions and crisis support. The system has set a mandate to scale system-wide by 2030 and raise persistence rates by two and a half percent for Pell-eligible and first-generation students.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And from beyond higher education, a new study surveying federal judges across the U.S. found that more than 60 percent of respondents reported using at least one A.I. tool in their judicial work. According to Northwestern Now, the research led by Northwestern University faculty surveyed five hundred two judges and collected one hundred twelve responses. Only about 22 percent use A.I. tools on a weekly or daily basis. Judges reported using A.I. tools primarily for conducting legal research and reviewing documents. The study found that about 45 percent of judges said A.I. training was not provided by court administration, and roughly a quarter have no official policy on A.I. use. Approximately 20 percent of judges formally prohibit A.I. use in their chambers, while one in three permit or encourage its use.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
